newsitem.title: UK: Political row roils Russia overseas debt, equity.
newsitem.headline: Political row roils Russia overseas debt, equity.

text.p: Russian debt and equities traded overseas slid sharply on Thursday as deep rifts appeared in President Boris Yeltsin's administration, although traders said some investors were locking in profits after strong gains.
"People are thinking it is worth giving up a potential two cents profit and taking 10 cents now," said a trader.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Thursday sought to defuse a bitter Kremlin power struggle by giving partial support to enemies of Alexander Lebed but rejecting claims the security chief was plotting to seize power.

Accusations against Lebed by Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov drove the price of Vneshekonomobank dollar debt -- foreign commercial loans to the former Soviet Union -- down three cents to 74 percent of face in morning trade.

But Vnesh later rebounded to 76 percent of face value, although that was well off a record 80 percent set earlier this month. At its peak, Russian debt had climbed 150 percent from the start of this year.
"Prices came back, so people who followed the herd lost out by selling at the bottom," said Stuart Brown, an analyst at Paribas Capital markets in London
The political row comes at a key time for Russia.

The country is on the verge of a Eurobond issue of up to $500 million and RAO Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas producer, is looking for $460 million via the issue of shares to be listed in London.
"All of these things seem to march forward quite nicely, interest rates are down and the country won a good rating from Standard & Poors," said Daiwa chief political analyst Susanne Schmidt.
In October, S&P assigned Russia a BB-minus long-term foreign currency debt rating, better than that for Brazil or Turkey.
It also said that "short periods of policy stress would not affect Russia's ability to service its debt", a fact which has reassured investors.
"There are a lot of people out there who are hungry for Russia risk," said Mark Cooke, a fund manager at Brunswick Capital Management in London.
In recent weeks financial markets have moved on rumours, rapidly denied, that Yeltsin had died.

"These rumours are different from the ones earlier in that they originated in the Russian stockmarket. Somebody, probably not one of the long-established players, had been caught short," said an economist at a leading European bank.
Other fund managers said that they had sought to buy on one day when the market was off 10 percent, but found it impossible.
"The rumour was out there and we tried to do something, but despite prices being marked down there were no sellers of stock," said one.
Analysts said there was a certain inevitability about a power struggle occuring while Yeltsin is not in full control.
Daiwa's Schmidt warned late last month that overlapping ministries would seek to consolidate their control ahead of the president's heart operation scheduled for next month.
Others say that Lebed has few options other than to make a big noise now if he wants to keep some of the reins of power.
"Lebed is the hostage of Yeltsin, not the other way round and he is very short on options. He either gets out or stays in and becomes compromised," said Brunswick's Cooke.
Although the rows in Yeltsin's kitchen cabinet look set to continue and detract from the work of governing the country, most foreign observers were sanguine.

"Can you see them all still at each other's throats in four years time? Despite all the shennanigans in the Kremlin, people take a view that this is a big country and it will sort itself out," said Daiwa's Schmidt. -- David Chance London newsroom 44 171 542 5887
